[QURTUBI-FULL:18:99-105/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعد | reports | In a Bukhari report, Saʿd says the worst losers are Jews and Christians, not the Khawarij: Jews denied Muhammad, and Christians denied Paradise’s food and drink; he called the Khawarij covenant-breakers and wicked.
[QURTUBI-FULL:18:99-105/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The question rebukes disbelievers who worship other than God: their efforts and hopes fail, making them the greatest losers in deeds.
[QURTUBI-FULL:18:99-105/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علي | reports | Ali identifies the worst losers as the Khawarij of Harura; on another occasion he names the monks in their cells, and tells Ibn al-Kawwa that he and his companions are meant.

[NASHR:v1p214/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | A reader must articulate each letter at its distinct point of origin and give it its proper qualities through practice until accurate pronunciation becomes natural.
[NASHR:v1p214/r10] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Ṣād, zāy, and sīn share articulation, softness, and whistling; ṣād is emphatic, zāy voiced, and sīn voiceless.

[NASHR:v1p214/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Letters sharing a point of articulation are distinguished by their qualities; letters sharing qualities are distinguished by their points of articulation.
[NASHR:v1p214/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Hamza and hāʾ share articulation, openness, and low tongue position; hamza alone is voiced and a stop.
[NASHR:v1p214/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | ʿAyn and ḥāʾ share articulation, openness, and low tongue position; ḥāʾ alone is voiceless and purely fricative.

[NASHR:v1p361/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | At a stop on words like يشاء, qasr is never allowed; nor is tawassut for a reader who uses full madd in continuation, while full madd can apply for one who uses tawassut.
[NASHR:v1p361/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Warsh must use full madd on al-samāʾ because the original madd cause remains and is strengthened by stopping; al-Azraq may not use qasr at pause.

[ALUSI-FULL:v16p47#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إرشاد العقل السليم | reports | The passage contrasts unbelievers’ intrinsically good acts, which they admire and expect reward for, with their intrinsically bad acts that they mistakenly deem good.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p45/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The passage answers those who worship useless idols as patrons and seek their favor, making their work and effort futile; the key rebuke is that they think they do well.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p45/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The question whether to inform them is an offer used ironically: the speaker will inform them regardless of their assent.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p45/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The wording shifts from direct address to third person, building curiosity before revealing that the losers are the listeners themselves.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p45/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The polytheists are addressed to rebuke them and alert them to the failure of their efforts.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p45/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The plural nūn in nunabbiʾukum may be God’s majestic plural, with narrative shift from expected he informs you.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p45/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Alternatively, the plural nūn may refer to the Messenger together with God, or to the Messenger and Muslims.
